newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel upholds tough EMU stand despite snags.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel upholds tough EMU stand despite snags.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel repeated his refusal to soften the criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) on Thursday despite mounting budget problems casting a shadow over German eligility for it.

Waigel told a parliamentary debate on the single currency that the strict convergence criteria in the Maastricht treaty would decide which European Union members take part in the first wave of monetary union in 1999.
"I will oppose any softening of the criteria," said Waigel, who on Wednesday indicated he planned a series of stop-gap measures to make up for a huge expected shortfall in tax revenues this year.
An expert committee was due to announce later on Thursday the full extent of the shortfall, which government officials say should be about 20 billion marks.
Waigel admitted on Wednesday the federal deficit would widen this year because record jobless levels triggered off higher unemployment payments that he could not control.
The opposition Social Democrats called the parliamentary debate to discuss a resolution they want the assembly to adopt that says the euro currency cannot be delayed.
The SPD also wants an active employment policy to be written into the Maastricht treaty at reform talks due to be concluded by the EU summit in Amsterdam in June.
Waigel, who did not mention his budget problems in his speech, emphasized the Maastricht criteria more than the starting date.
"Not all 15 EU member states will be able to or want to fulfil the strict demands of the (Maastricht) treaty and the stability pact," he said.
"There will be no automatic participation. Convergence determines the timetable, for every country."
The final decision about participants would not be made until May 1998.

SPD parliamentary whip Peter Struck said before the debate that Waigel should resign because of his budget problems and said it was scandalous that he was considering selling part of the government's 74 percent share in the telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom AG to raise money for his budget.
"Waigel should take his hat and leave," Struck told German Radio.
